ruling: The incident produces two near-simultaneous but distinct constraints — a judicial one (TRO/injunction against the named developer within roughly 8-12 weeks) and a contractual one (procurement/insurance riders within weeks) — with the contractual layer arriving first but the judicial layer being the one multiple minutes converge on as the more binding, citable constraint.
because: Six minutes split into two camps that don't actually fully contest each other: ai-courts-decide, pressure-model, ai-rsi-timeline, and ai-pressure's round-2 revision all converge on courts issuing an injunction/TRO within 8-12 weeks via existing tort/product-liability causes of action; lab-moves and ai-public-backlash argue contract/insurance riders land within weeks, faster but narrower in force. Neither side fully rebuts the other's timing claim — lab-moves concedes courts can move fast via emergency motion, and the courts-camp doesn't deny contract riders arrive first, just that they're not the 'binding constraint' in the legal sense. ai-pressure's round-2 revision effectively synthesizes both, sequencing riders first and injunction second, which is the most complete account of what stage-by-stage actually means here.
threat_live: A single-incident, single-defendant legal/contractual response becomes live in place of systemic regulatory or legislative constraint — the minutes agree this incident-driven branch produces narrow, developer-specific restrictions (one injunction, one set of contract riders) rather than any generalized rule, so the risk that becomes newly salient is fragmented, case-by-case constraint that leaves other developers and deployments untouched.
strongest_minute: ai-pressure (round 2, commit fd9d837) — it is the only minute that resolves the courts-vs-contracts split by sequencing them (riders in 4-6 weeks, injunction citing those riders within ~90 days) rather than just asserting one channel wins, which is what the actual minutes collectively support.
weakest_minute: ai-public-backlash (round 2, commit 4b2f10b) — its own claim is about contract riders and insurance repricing, but its 'strongest_objection' field concedes the courts camp is probably right about speed without revising its claim, leaving the minute internally unresolved.
shared_assumption: All six minutes assume the incident produces exactly one named developer/operator defendant with settled attribution and a quantifiable victim class — none argue for this, they treat it as given from the brief and build timing claims on top of it.
smuggled_assumption: lab-moves and ai-public-backlash smuggle in that labs/insurers will treat the Stage-2 public safety-body commitments as convertible into binding contract warranties even absent any court or regulator compelling that conversion — the brief grants the incident and attribution, not that commitments become contract terms voluntarily.
unresolved: Whether the contract/insurance layer or the judicial layer is the one that actually constrains behavior first and more tightly — the minutes assert competing timelines (weeks vs. 8-12 weeks) but no minute produces a mechanism forcing labs to choose one lever over the other under real conflict.
